name: str_split
title: Split up a string into pieces

origin.description: Split each string in a character vector into a varying number of pieces.
origin.usage: str_split(string, pattern, n = Inf, simplify = FALSE)

arguments.name: string
arguments.text: Input vector. Either a character vector, or something coercible to one.

arguments.name: pattern
arguments.text: Pattern to look for. The default interpretation is a regular expression. regex() sets the flags. fixed() compares literal text. coll() uses Unicode collation for a locale. boundary() matches character, word, line, and sentence boundaries. The empty string "" is equivalent to boundary("character").

arguments.name: n
arguments.text: Maximum number of pieces to return. Inf, the default, uses every split. This is the maximum length of each result. A larger n does not pad.

arguments.name: simplify
arguments.text: FALSE, the default, returns a list of character vectors. TRUE returns a character matrix padded with "". NA returns that matrix padded with missing values.

origin.details: string and pattern are checked with vctrs::vec_size_common. A length of 1 recycles, including to length 0, and any other two lengths must agree. n of Inf is passed to stringi as -1. A positive n keeps n - 1 pieces and the unsplit remainder. The pattern type selects stri_split_regex, stri_split_fixed, stri_split_coll, or stri_split_boundaries, and the modifier's option list is passed through. A plain character vector is a regular expression, unless it is exactly "", which is a character boundary. A boundary pattern passes its break-iterator options and not the missing string it stores. simplify FALSE does not pad. simplify TRUE pads with "" and simplify NA pads with NA.
origin.value: A list the same length as string and pattern, containing character vectors. With simplify TRUE or NA, a character matrix with one row per string.
origin.example:
fruits <- c(
  "apples and oranges and pears and bananas",
  "pineapples and mangos and guavas"
)
str_split(fruits, " and ")
str_split(fruits, " and ", simplify = TRUE)
str_split(fruits, " and ", n = 3)
str_split(fruits, " and ", n = 2)
str_split(fruits, " and ", n = 5)

translation.description: Split each string into a list of pieces.

arguments.name: string
arguments.text: A string, stringi._na.NA, or a list of those. None is an empty character vector.

arguments.name: pattern
arguments.text: A string, a list of strings, or a Pattern from fixed, coll, regex, or boundary. A plain string is a regular expression. "" and [""] are a character boundary. A one-element tuple of "" is treated as that list.

arguments.name: n
arguments.text: Maximum number of pieces. float("inf") becomes -1 and keeps every piece. A positive whole number keeps that many pieces and does not pad when simplify is False. 1.0 is accepted. 0, a fraction, TRUE, and NA are errors.

arguments.name: simplify
arguments.text: False returns a list of lists. True returns one row per string, padded with "". stringi._na.NA pads with NA.

translation.details: check_lengths is stringr._size.check_lengths. pattern_type and pattern_opts choose the splitter and its options. empty and bound call stri_split_boundaries. fixed, regex, and coll call stri_split_fixed, stri_split_regex, and stri_split_coll with the modifier options. The boundary Pattern stores NA; that value is not used as a delimiter. A positive n is the stringi limit: n - 1 finished pieces and the remainder. Names on the R result are not attached.
translation.value: A list of lists of strings. Missing pieces are stringi._na.NA. With simplify True or NA, each inner list is one row of the character matrix.
translation.example:
from stringr.split import str_split

fruits = [
    "apples and oranges and pears and bananas",
    "pineapples and mangos and guavas",
]
print(str_split(fruits, " and "))
print(str_split(fruits, " and ", simplify=True))
print(str_split(fruits, " and ", n=3))
print(str_split(fruits, " and ", n=2))
print(str_split(fruits, " and ", n=5))
